title: Counting Collections
strapline: Grab a handful, guess, then count them out — number that lives in the things children love to gather.
intent: Children count real, appealing objects with one-to-one correspondence and know the last number is the total.
Children estimate, then check, building a feel for how many and how close their guess was.
Children find their own ways to organise a count — lining up, grouping, using a frame.
Children compare collections — more, fewer, the same — and share them out fairly.
Children see number as a natural part of gathering, sorting and playing, not a worksheet.
implementation: Stock beautiful, countable collections — conkers, buttons, gems, shells, pinecones — in generous amounts.
Invite an estimate first — grab a handful, guess how many — then count to check together.
Count aloud with a touch per object and celebrate the last number: 'one, two, three, four — FOUR!'
Offer bowls, frames and trays so children discover ways to organise a count and not lose track.
Make deliberate miscounts for children to catch — count one twice, skip one, get the total wrong.
Compare two collections and share them out — more, fewer, one each, is it fair?
Weave counting into real jobs all day — cups, coats, steps, register — so number is everywhere.
key_questions: How many do you think you're holding — shall we count to check?
Was your guess more or fewer than the real number?
How could you count them without losing your place?
Which bowl has more — how do you know?
Have we got enough for everyone to have one?

impact.text: Children count objects with one-to-one correspondence and know the last number is the total.
Children estimate and then check, building a feel for how many.
Children find their own ways to organise a count — lining up, grouping, using a frame.
Children compare collections using more, fewer and the same, and share fairly.
Children count naturally in real jobs — cups, coats, steps — through the day.
Children sort their collections by their own rules as they count.

enhancements: Generous collections of conkers, buttons, gems, shells and pinecones.
Bowls, sorting trays, frames and number tracks to organise counts.
A mystery bag for grab-and-estimate games.
Numeral cards to match to the counted amounts.
A 'guess and check' recording strip with pictures.
Two bowls and a fair-share challenge for comparing and dealing out.
Loose parts refreshed from seasonal walks to keep the collection fresh.

playing_exploring: Children handle beautiful things because they want to — the counting follows the fascination.
Open collections invite children to invent their own counting games.
active_learning: Checking a guess and being close is a satisfaction children chase again.
Children persist to count a big collection right, without losing their place.
creating_thinking: Children invent strategies — grouping, lining up, using frames — to keep track.
They reason about which is more and how to make it fair.
